newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: MOTOR RACING-SCHUMACHER SET TO LEAD GENUINE FERRARI CHALLENGE.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-SCHUMACHER SET TO LEAD GENUINE FERRARI CHALLENGE.

text.p: Three new arrivals have given double world champion Michael Schumacher an air of increased maturity and authority this year as he sets about leading Ferrari's challenge for their first world title in 18 years.

Firstly, the birth of his first daughter last month has made him a father for the first time as he and wife Corinna settle into their new home on the shores of Lake Geneva in Switzerland after leaving Monaco last autumn.

The second change is more likely to maintain his edge, his interest and his hunger in Grand Prix racing because this winter he has welcomed his competitive younger brother Ralf, 21, into the Formula One paddock as a rival.
Ralf will be racing for Jordan, the team with whom Schumacher himself started his career, albeit for only one race, in 1991.
Thirdly, Ferrari, at Schumacher's prompting, last December recruited Ross Brawn as technical director and followed that by signing Rory Byrne as chief designer.
Both men worked closely with Schumacher at Benetton when he won the drivers' world titles of 1994 and 1995 and were seen as the architects of the Benetton success story of the early 1990s.

But Brawn, Schumacher and the rest of Ferrari's highly-fancied and heavily-financed team have gone on record before the season-opening race in Melbourne on March 9 as saying they cannot win the title this year.

"We have improved a lot and I am sure we will have better reliability this year but I cannot say we will win races, or enough races, to challenge for the championship," said Schumacher whose pre-season testing has been hampered by problems.

"I am not convinced we have made enough progress. Williams are still much faster than us and they will stay there. We are in the thick of the teams fighting for points and occasional podium finishes. That's all.

"Last year, I didn't expect to win races. So it was wonderful to win three, particularly one at Monza. I wanted to do well and to prove myself because when you change teams people say that you are proving yourself.

"If you go to a different team you can prove your ability. You find out about how much you can give and how much you can achieve. So to succeed as I did in a few races for Ferrari in a difficult season was very satisfying."
Helping Ferrari develop from a sleeping Formula One giant into genuine title-challengers will be at least a three-year project in his view.
"That is what I have always said and I see no reason to change my mind," he said. "I hope we win some more races and finish in the points but I don't think we will win enough for the title."
The 28-year-old, who has always been regarded as the fittest driver ever in Formula One, has also changed his training routine this winter.

He said: "My exercising is more effective but less demanding than it used to be. I used to do 150 push-ups a day but I found that there are other exercises for the same muscles which are just as effective.
"We need to do a lot of exercise to stay fit but we need to do it without damaging our bodies at the same time."

This year, in addition to his commitments to Ferrari and his family, Schumacher will also be called to give evidence as a witness at the Senna death trial at Imola. It was Senna's death that removed his main rival and enabled him to become so quickly established as the world number one.

Asked if he felt sad that he did not have anyone of the status of Senna around to test himself against any longer, Schumacher responded: "Yes, I think there is a sense of loss in this but I don't see myself as the best driver in the world.
"There are many drivers in the world who are still very competitive and there are many new ones coming through who will be better than me."

He identified fellow-German Heinz-Harald Frentzen as his biggest threat this year now that he has joined Williams as team-mate to Canadian Jacques Villeneuve. He explained why. "It is fair to say that speed-wise, we have been quite equal.
"From my knowledge of him from the last few years, I would rate him very highly, perhaps as the favourite. He had become quicker and quicker and that should be the case again now he is with Williams.
"But if things are not going well, then it is going to be very difficult for him.
"He is with the team that we all want to beat. Normally, cars develop and they either get better or they stay the same. But they don't usually get worse, so I believe he should be in a strong car.
"I am doing as much as possible for Ferrari in my car and I will push as much as I can, so long as the car is not damaged or unreliable."
